title: The Rise of the "Engineered Apprenticeship"
author: Philippa Hardman
summary: Philippa Hardman argues that the course, long the default unit of workplace learning, is being displaced by what she calls the engineered apprenticeship -- deliberately designed practice-and-feedback loops that replace the informal mentorship AI has automated away. She profiles four live examples: Big Law firms rehearsing depositions with an AI simulator called DepoSim, an international arbitration firm using an AI tool called Atelier to rehearse cross-examination, KPMG's TaxSIM simulating an entire tax career for roughly 10,000 professionals, and Deloitte/PwC rebuilding their graduate schemes around realistic scenarios and early AI-review responsibilities. Across all four, she identifies a repeating anatomy: a practice loop of attempt-compare-retry, expert reasoning deliberately captured rather than absorbed by proximity, and a target of teaching juniors to judge AI output from their first week. Citing research that AI narrows the novice-expert gap on routine tasks but widens it on judgment-heavy ones, Hardman argues L&D's job hasn't shrunk in the AI era but expanded by an order of magnitude. She closes with UK and US salary data showing roles built around AI-driven capability design already paying roughly 50% more than traditional course-design roles.
points: Four case studies (Big Law depositions, arbitration cross-examination, KPMG's TaxSIM, Deloitte/PwC graduate redesigns) show elite knowledge-work employers replacing the course with AI-driven simulate-and-feedback loops.

The common anatomy across all four builds: a practice loop (attempt, compare to expert, retry), captured expert reasoning as the fuel, and a target of teaching juniors to judge AI output from day one.

AI narrows the novice-expert gap on routine tasks but widens it on judgment-heavy tasks, which is why organizations are front-loading scepticism and review skills that used to arrive around year five of a career.
The salary data is the sharpest signal: roles framed around AI, consulting, and capability-building pay roughly 50% more than traditional course-design roles in both the UK and US markets cited.
quotes: AI has removed the way employees used to build their expertise: years of routine work, powered by lots of feedback and observation of more senior colleagues doing the work well. That's exactly the work AI now automates -- and, to a large extent, makes invisible.
Six major US firms -- Orrick, K&L Gates, McDermott, Littler, Taft and Brownstein -- piloted DepoSim this year, an AI simulator for depositions built by AltaClaro with Verbit.
KPMG's build is the scale story. TaxSIM, built with Centaurian AI, is designed to give junior tax professionals the skills that used to take years of repetitive client work
On routine, well-defined tasks, AI narrows the gap between novices and experts
For decades, L&D's design remit covered roughly 10% of how people actually built capability -- the formal course layer -- while the other 90% designed itself, invisibly, inside the work.
Roles focused on course design and production carry a median salary of £35,000 in the UK in 2026, while roles framed around AI, consulting and capability-building pay a median rate of £52,551.
